Android from the foundation · Puzzle 6 of 15

Each app is its own user

The kernel keeps processes apart while they run. Android also keeps each app's files apart, by giving every app its own identity.

The problem

In puzzle 0, two running apps couldn't touch each other's memory. But apps also keep files on the phone, like a bank's saved accounts. When the bank app isn't even running, what stops a game from opening its files?

See it

Save this diagram as a GIF

The building block

Linux was built for computers shared by many people, so it keeps accounts apart. A Linux account isn't necessarily a person: it's an identity the kernel uses to decide who owns which files. Android reuses that: at install time, every app gets its own account, with its own user ID, or UID. The UID stays the same for as long as the app is installed. Files the app creates belong to its UID, and every process of the app carries that UID, so the kernel always knows who's asking.

The kernel checks the UID on every file and every process. The result is the sandbox: walls around each app's files and memory that no app can switch off, because the kernel enforces them.

The analogy

Every house has its own key. The kernel is the lock on every door: it opens only for the right key.

Check yourself

The bank app isn't running. Can the game open the bank's saved files now?

Not quite. The walls aren't guarded by the bank app; the kernel checks the key on every file, running or not.

Right. The kernel checks the UID whether or not the owner is running.

Who enforces the sandbox?

Right. The kernel enforces it, so no app can switch it off.

Not quite. The town hall manages screens. The walls around files and memory are the kernel's job.

Not quite. If apps had to behave, a hostile app simply wouldn't. The kernel checks every access, whatever the app does.

What's the difference between a UID and a process?

Right. One app, one UID; its process comes and goes.

Not quite. The UID is the key, given at install. The process is the running house, started and ended many times.

Sources

  • Android Open Source Project: Application sandbox

What you now know

Every app gets its own UID, its key. The kernel checks that key on every file, so one app can never open another's private files: the sandbox.
